summary: RFC 8110 describes Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, which lets clients without credentials connect to a network with encrypted traffic. This informational document transfers maintenance and further development of the protocol to the IEEE 802.11 Working Group, and updates RFC 8110 to say so.

eli5.summary: A wireless scrambling trick was invented in one group, and now a different group that makes the Wi-Fi rules will look after it from here on.

questions: is owe still developed by the ietf
subtitle: Future work on Opportunistic Wireless Encryption moves from the IETF to the IEEE 802.11 Working Group.

tldr.problem: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), specified in RFC 8110, is an IEEE 802.11 mode, and the IEEE 802.11 Working Group asked to maintain and develop it so it stays in sync with IEEE protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This document records the IETF's concurrence that future work on OWE will occur in the IEEE 802.11 Working Group, and says the protocol will be duplicated there so that the IEEE document alone is enough to implement it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8110 is updated only by a note that further development happens in the IEEE; no protocol change is made.

today: RFC 9672 is an Informational document that updates RFC 8110. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Background on OWE
sections.content:
Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), defined in RFC 8110, is a mode of opportunistic security (RFC 7435) for IEEE Std 802.11. It encrypts the wireless medium without authentication, so clients without credentials can still connect with encrypted traffic.

The text says RFC 8110, also known as "Wi-Fi Enhanced Open", has been widely implemented and deployed since publication.
sections.eli5: OWE scrambles what you send over Wi-Fi even when you never typed a password. It is a lock that anyone can use without a key.

sections.title: Transfer of Maintenance
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.11 Working Group requested the ability to maintain and develop OWE, citing a liaison statement from May 2024, to ensure that the protocol remains in sync with the IEEE protocols. This document represents concurrence that future work on OWE will now occur in that group.

The OWE protocol of RFC 8110 will be duplicated by the IEEE 802.11 Working Group, so that the IEEE document alone will be enough to implement, maintain and modify the protocol under IEEE policies and procedures.
sections.eli5: The Wi-Fi rule makers asked to take over looking after this trick, and the IETF said yes. They will keep their own copy of the instructions.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The document only notes that future work will occur in the IEEE, so it introduces no new security considerations. It also has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Nothing about how the lock works has changed, only who looks after it, so nothing new to worry about.
